articles.description:
As agentic systems mature, I keep getting pulled into the same discussion:
Should we build an “agent exchange”?
A marketplace.
It’s a reasonable instinct. Platforms are tangible, fundable, and easy to explain. But if we look at how the internet itself scaled, a different pattern emerges; one that is worth revisiting before we hard-code the future of agent ecosystems.
The most durable digital ecosystems have not been built on centralized exchanges. They have been built on open discovery standards, which then enabled many kinds of platforms to emerge naturally on top.
That distinction matters.
The early web did not begin with a global website directory. Instead, it began with a small set of boring but powerful primitives. DNS solved naming. HTTP solved retrieval. Well-known locations solved …

I recently finished building a promotional engine for an e-commerce platform. The logic was simple: A "Flash Sale" coupon that expires in 2 hours.
I wrote the logic, tested it, and deployed it. It worked perfectly. Then, I decided to switch hats. I stopped being the developer and started being the bad actor.

The Result? The coupon, which should have expired, became valid again. The "Expired" button turned back into "Apply." My backend accepted the order.
I had accidentally committed the cardinal sin of web development: I trusted the client.

articles.author: Anish Jhaveri
articles.description:
I just shipped an automated lead qualification system for a B2B SaaS client. The whole build took 7 days from kickoff to production deployment.
The sales team was manually reviewing 50+ demo requests per week. About half were unqualified (students, competitors, tire-kickers). They needed automation that could:
Enrich leads with company data
Score based on ICP fit

Route qualified leads to sales, others to nurture campaigns
n8n for workflow orchestration
Clearbit for company enrichment
Custom scoring logic (revenue, employee count, tech stack)
HubSpot for CRM integration
70% of leads auto-qualified (no human touch needed)
Sales team saves 15 hours/week
2x faster response time to hot leads
$0 in ongoing costs (self-hosted n8n)
Don't try to score leads with just email and name. Enrich first with:
Company size
Revenue estimates

Tech stack
Funding status
Started with complex ML scoring. Scrapped it. Went with simple if/then rules:
Company size > 50 employees? +10 points
Uses Salesforce? +5 points
Has funding? +5 points
Edge cases will break your automation. Build in a "needs review" queue for:
Scores between 40-60 (gray area)
Missing enrichment data
VIP domains (investors, partners)
I wrote a detailed walkthrough with code snippets and n8n workflow screenshots here:
Lead Qualification System Breakdown
Happy to answer questions about the build, n8n workflows, or automation architecture in general!
articles.title: I Built a Lead Qualification System in 7 Days Using n8n + AI
